items.passage: "Put that down before the stew scorches," Wenhua said, without turning from the stove. Sequoia folded the envelope twice, then a third time, as if smaller paper might hold fewer words. The galley had been salvaged from a decommissioned steamer and hauled inland decades ago, and on windy nights the whole trailer creaked like it still remembered water. The letter was addressed to her aunt, in a hand Sequoia did not know, and she had read only the first line before her pulse began knocking in her ears. She wondered, briefly, who in the world still wrote to Wenhua at all. Then the ladle struck the pot rim, sharp as a gavel, and Sequoia slid the envelope under the flour tin. Outside, the mesa held the last orange light, and the onions hissed in the pan.

items.passage: Some objects refuse to leave with their owners. When I bought the house above the tide pools in Maui, Mika, the gardener, came with it, and so did a cracked snorkel mask hanging on a nail by the salt-water pool. I offered to throw it out. Mika looked at the mask the way one looks at a sleeping dog, then said that Moira, who had lived here thirty years, used it every dawn, even after she could no longer swim far. I laughed, a little embarrassed, and admitted I had already tried it on. Mika laughed too, which surprised us both. Now I glance at that nail whenever the tide fills the pool, and I find myself rinsing the mask, though I never wear it. Mika trims the hibiscus along the wall on Thursdays.

items.passage: Tbilisi in February smelled of wet stone and glue, at least inside the bookbinder's workshop where our chess club met after closing. Dainius walked in that evening as though eleven years were a short errand. He set his coat on the press and asked whether the board by the window was free. Nobody answered. I was Tatiana, his oldest rival, so the question was really mine, and I found my hands squaring a stack of signatures that were already square. He offered no reason for leaving, and I did not ask; asking would have meant admitting I had counted the years. Still, I pushed the white pieces toward him, the way I always had when he was losing. Behind us the binder pulled thread through a spine, slow and even.

items.passage: By four this morning I was already at the bakery, Esperanza, kneading before the ovens were warm, because I could not stay in the house another hour. You asked how the division went. On paper, perfectly: my brother takes the upper floor and the boathouse, I keep the kitchen and our mother's piano, and the lawyer called it a model settlement. I suppose I should be glad that no one shouted. Yet when I carried my half of the plates down the stairs, each stack seemed to weigh more than the last, and I caught myself setting out two cups out of habit. Snow is falling on the harbor now in Tromso, and the first loaves are browning. I will write again when the shop closes. Yours, Jens

items.passage: I unfolded the scarf on the barge's narrow deck while the Red River slid brown and slow beneath us in Hanoi. It was mustard yellow, the one color I had refused to wear since childhood, and Faris, my younger brother's tutor, watched my face as though it were an exam he had studied for. My brother must have told him yellow was my favorite; my brother thought jokes were a form of love. I tied the scarf at my throat and said it matched the lanterns on the far bank. Faris let out a breath and began explaining, too quickly, how well the boy was doing with fractions. I nodded at every fraction. Along the bank, a woman was hanging fish to dry on a line of bamboo poles.

items.passage: Agnes had not expected anyone to find her in the courtyard, where the fountain had been dry since before her family moved to Colombo. She was scraping lichen from its rim with a thumbnail when Rukhsana sat down beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Neither of them mentioned the assembly, or the speech Agnes had forgotten halfway through in front of the whole school. Instead Rukhsana opened a paper cone of roasted peanuts and tipped half of them into Agnes's palm, the way she had every afternoon since they were seven. Agnes ate one, then another, and felt her face cool. Overhead, a crow walked the length of the wall and dropped a twig into the empty basin.

items.passage: When Freja arrived at the community garden in Rotterdam, Ingeborg was already kneeling between the bean rows, as she did every Saturday before rehearsal. Freja held out the letter from the Vienna academy, and Ingeborg glanced at it only long enough to say, You are still flat on the high E. Then she handed Freja a trowel and pointed to the weeds she always left for her. Freja knelt and worked beside her without speaking, though twice she caught the older woman watching her hands instead of the soil. Later, when Freja stood to go, Ingeborg pressed a jar of last year's honey into her coat pocket and turned back to the beans before Freja could thank her. items.passage: Years later, I still think of the night shifts at the old signal station outside Marrakesh, where Hamza and I watched a beacon that no ship would ever need. That spring I had borrowed money from him for my mother's medicine, and every Friday I held out a folded envelope. Every Friday he pushed it back across the desk and asked, instead, whether I could take his last two hours so he could see his daughter before school. items.passage: Diesel and wet umbrellas: that is how the bus depot in Taipei smelled the morning I saw Kamal again, twenty years after we last sang together at the harbor theater. She was standing at the ticket window, arguing softly with the clerk, and when I reached the counter he told me my fare to Tainan had already been paid. I turned, but Kamal was studying the timetable with great concentration. I bought two cups of hot soy milk from the kiosk and set one on the bench beside her without a word, the way she used to leave water by my music stand. She lifted it and nodded, still reading departure times. Somewhere behind us an engine coughed, and pigeons rose from the rafters in a gray sheet.

items.passage: I took the last night bus out of Marseille with my violin across my knees and, in my coat pocket, the cake of rosin Remy had given me at my first lesson. It was cracked down the middle now, worn into a shallow valley by eight years of his insistence that I bow slower, slower. The audition in Paris was in the morning, and the teacher there had already written that he used only a newer, softer rosin; he would supply it. Twice, as the bus wound along the coast, I took Remy's cake out, meaning to leave it on the seat beside me. Twice I put it back. Somewhere past Aix, I rubbed my thumb along the crack until it was warm, and I did not sleep. The windows showed only my own reflection, and behind it, the dark.

items.passage: "Stand still and they'll forget you're here," Ivy said, working the bellows of the smoker until gray clouds drifted over the hives. Hortense obeyed, as she had obeyed in Ivy's classroom thirty years before. The bees grew sluggish and mild, and Ivy lifted out a heavy frame without a single sting. "Smoke doesn't hurt them," Ivy said. "It only tells them not to worry." Hortense remembered the ginger biscuits Ivy used to slip her after school, always on the afternoons the headmaster called her father in. She had thought them comfort. Now, watching the drowsy bees surrender their honey, she wondered what else had been lifted out of that house while she was busy chewing. Ivy offered her a jar of the honey, and Hortense, after a moment, took it.

items.passage:
Three rules my uncle Dewi kept at the loom:
count every thread, owe no one, trust no rival.
We owed the cooperative in Bologna
more than a winter's linen could repay,
and Nora, at the next loom, wove faster than us both.
He called her the competition. I called her nothing.
But when our warp snapped on the morning of the market,
it was Nora who knotted it, thread across thread,
her weft running sideways through our long, straight lines.
Warp holds still; weft crosses over.
Neither one alone is cloth.
By evening the bolt was finished, and my uncle,
counting, lost his place, and laughed, and counted again.
items.question: In the poem, the warp and weft most likely represent which of the following?
options: How opposing forces can bind together into something stronger
The uncle's strict rules for keeping his accounts in order
The debt that grows heavier as the long winter continues
The rivalry that drives each weaver to work ever faster
items.explanation: 삼촌은 Nora를 경쟁자로 여겼지만, 날실이 끊어지자 그녀가 실을 가로질러 묶어 천을 완성하게 돕는다. 가만히 있는 날실과 가로지르는 씨실 중 어느 하나만으로는 천이 되지 않는다는 구절은 대립하던 쪽이 결합해 하나를 이루는 것을 상징한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 첫 행의 규칙, C는 빚, D는 경쟁이라는 지문 소재만 가져왔을 뿐 실의 이미지가 가리키는 결합과는 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Havana's outskirts still had a post office with a brass telegraph key bolted to the counter, though no message had passed through it in decades. I had come there as a new teacher, Roshane, to teach Morse code to anyone who wanted to learn, and the only one who came was Valentina, fourteen, arms folded, certain the key was a museum piece. Its knob was worn bright, a shallow dip pressed into it by thumbs I would never meet. On the first day Valentina refused to touch it. On the fifth, she tapped out her own name, badly, and set her thumb exactly in that hollow without noticing. By the end of the month she was correcting my rhythm. When I left, the postmistress asked whether to remove the key at last. Valentina answered before I could, and the key stayed.
items.question: In the text, the worn hollow on the telegraph key most likely represents which of the following?
options: The uselessness of a machine that no longer sends any messages
A skill handed down through many people, now reaching Valentina
Valentina's stubborn resistance to learning from a stranger
The postmistress's wish to modernize the old post office
items.explanation: 손잡이의 움푹한 자리는 화자가 결코 만나지 못할 많은 사람의 엄지가 남긴 흔적이며, Valentina가 무심코 바로 그 자리에 엄지를 얹으면서 그녀도 그 계보에 들어간다. 이후 그녀가 리듬을 고쳐 주고 열쇠를 남기게 하는 장면도 사라져 가는 기술이 이어짐을 보여 준다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 수십 년간 쓰이지 않았다는 사실만, C는 처음의 거부만, D는 우체국장의 질문만 가져와 상징의 의미를 놓쳤다.

items.passage: After the winter my father chipped Wilhelmina's blue serving bowl, he turned it every morning so the broken edge faced the kitchen wall. Wilhelmina ran the boarding house in Bergen and counted her dishes the way other people count money, yet she never seemed to see the chip. I saw it. I was eleven and stubborn and had been told I was wrong about everything that year, so I said nothing, which felt like winning. Each morning I watched him rotate the bowl before Leopoldina, the cook, filled it with porridge, and each morning, after he left, I checked that the edge still faced the wall. Neither of us ever spoke of it. When we moved out in spring, he lifted the bowl last, turned it once more, and set it down exactly as it had been.
items.question: In the text, the chipped bowl most likely represents which of the following?
options: The father's careless habits that annoyed the landlady
The family's poverty during their years at the house
A mistake that father and son silently agree to hide
The son's wish to expose his father's carelessness
items.explanation: 아버지는 매일 아침 깨진 쪽을 벽으로 돌려 놓고, 그것을 본 유일한 사람인 아들은 말하지 않은 채 깨진 쪽이 여전히 벽을 향하는지 확인한다. 두 사람이 끝까지 그 일을 입에 올리지 않고, 떠나는 날 아버지가 그릇을 한 번 더 돌려 두는 장면은 둘이 말없이 공유한 비밀을 보여 준다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 집주인이 흠을 알아채지 못했다는 내용과 맞지 않고, B는 근거가 없으며, D는 아들이 침묵을 지킨 것과 정반대다.

items.passage: Cornwall's smallest harbor, so the old tale goes, held one boat that belonged to two people: old Ephraim and the granddaughter who had come to learn his tongue. A merchant named Albert offered gold for the boat, enough to fill both their pockets. Ephraim did not answer. Instead he handed the girl a torn net and taught her the old word for each knot as she mended it: one for the knot that holds, one for the knot that forgives, one for the knot that remembers. All winter she mended and spoke, until the words came to her without thinking. In spring Albert returned with more gold. The girl looked at the net spread across the seawall, every knot with a name, and told him the boat was not for sale. Ephraim only nodded and went down to the water.
items.question: In the text, the mended net most likely represents which of the following?
options: The hard labor that the girl secretly wishes to escape
The wealth that Albert hopes to gain from the harbor
The damage that the old boat has suffered over time
The heritage that binds the girl to Ephraim's language
items.explanation: Ephraim은 팔지 말라고 말하는 대신 그물을 건네고, 매듭마다 붙는 옛말을 손녀에게 가르친다. 겨울 내내 그물을 고치며 말이 자연스러워진 손녀가 모든 매듭에 이름이 있는 그물을 보고 배를 팔지 않겠다고 결정하므로, 그물은 할아버지의 언어와 유산으로 이어진 유대를 상징한다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A는 수선을 고된 노동으로만 보았고, B는 상인의 금화, C는 찢어진 그물이라는 표면 소재만 가져왔다.

items.passage: Bogdan, the caretaker of the school gymnasium in Riga, let the two women in after hours, as he had every Thursday since the mother's knees began to fail. The daughter swept the long floor while her mother sat on the lowest bench and wound the climbing ropes, slowly, the way she had done for thirty years. In nine days the daughter would board a plane for Toronto and not come back. Neither of them mentioned it. Instead the mother asked Bogdan to turn off the radio, and when the daughter dropped the broom, the clatter rang out alone in the high room. Her mother did not look up. She was practicing the silence, Bogdan thought, the way the girls on the team once practiced a vault before the real meet. He locked the doors behind them at ten.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “practicing the silence” most nearly suggests that the mother is
options: trying to calm her daughter before a stressful journey.
showing irritation at the noise of the dropped broom.
preparing herself for life after her daughter is gone.
training herself to ignore Bogdan's many interruptions.
items.explanation: 딸은 아흐레 뒤 토론토로 떠나 돌아오지 않을 예정이고, 어머니는 라디오를 끄게 한 뒤 빗자루 소리가 텅 빈 체육관에 홀로 울려도 고개를 들지 않는다. 체조 선수들이 실제 대회 전에 도마를 연습하듯 한다는 비유는 어머니가 딸이 없는 조용한 삶을 미리 익히고 있음을 뜻한다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 딸을 진정시킨다는 근거가 없고, B는 소리에 대한 짜증으로 오해했으며, D는 Bogdan이 방해한다는 내용이 지문에 없다.

items.passage: Although they had not spoken in a month, Imani and Themba both arrived at the kite-maker's yard in Addis Ababa on the morning of the festival, each pretending to have come for something else. The festival contract, the one that would have filled both their ovens all year, had gone to a hotel kitchen across the city after each baker's sample arrived late. Themba said Imani had kept the only van. Imani said Themba had never once been on time. Overhead, the kite-maker's children ran with paper hawks and bright diamonds, and a gust tore one of the diamonds loose. That contract, Themba said quietly, was a kite with no string. They watched the loose diamond rise, wobbling, over the eucalyptus trees until it was only a speck.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a kite with no string” most nearly suggests that the contract was
options: a fragile agreement that the bakers could still easily repair.
a festival honor that only the kite-maker had power to grant.
a minor opportunity hardly worth the bakers' long argument.
a chance that had drifted beyond either baker's control.
items.explanation: 계약은 두 제빵사의 견본이 모두 늦게 도착해 다른 호텔 주방으로 넘어갔고, 둘은 서로에게 책임을 돌린다. 줄이 끊긴 연은 붙잡을 수 없이 멀어지는 것이므로, 이 비유는 계약이 이미 두 사람의 손을 떠났음을 뜻한다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A는 쉽게 되돌릴 수 있다고 해 비유와 반대이고, B는 연 장인을 끌어들인 오독이며, C는 일 년 내내 오븐을 채웠을 계약이라는 서술과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage:
Once, in a Galician spring, the river climbed
into the cellar of the old clinic, and Rafael,
the night nurse, waded down with a lantern
to carry up the jars of plum preserve
he had meant as a gift for Esteban in bed seven.
Esteban, who could not lift a spoon by then,
looked at the dripping jar a long time
and pushed it back across the blanket.
Keep it, he said. You saved it. It is yours.
Rafael set it on the sill and understood:
in that room where the water kept rising,
the old man's pride still kept its head above water.
The rain went on all night against the shutters.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “kept its head above water” most nearly suggests that Esteban's pride
options: survived despite his growing weakness and dependence.
made him fear that the flood would reach his room.
turned into anger at Rafael for entering the cellar.
gave him hope of recovering enough to leave the clinic.
items.explanation: Esteban은 숟가락도 들 수 없을 만큼 쇠약했지만, Rafael이 물에 잠긴 지하실에서 건져 온 선물을 고맙다고 받지 않고 네가 구했으니 네 것이라며 돌려준다. 물이 차오르는 방이라는 배경과 겹친 이 비유는 몸이 무너져 가는 상황에서도 그의 자존심이 꺾이지 않고 버티고 있음을 뜻한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 홍수를 문자 그대로 읽었고, C는 분노의 근거가 없으며, D는 회복에 대한 희망을 지문이 보여 주지 않는다.

### lit40-medium-02-001 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood
[지문]
"Put that down before the stew scorches," Wenhua said, without turning from the stove. Sequoia folded the envelope twice, then a third time, as if smaller paper might hold fewer words. The galley had been salvaged from a decommissioned steamer and hauled inland decades ago, and on windy nights the whole trailer creaked like it still remembered water. The letter was addressed to her aunt, in a hand Sequoia did not know, and she had read only the first line before her pulse began knocking in her ears. She wondered, briefly, who in the world still wrote to Wenhua at all. Then the ladle struck the pot rim, sharp as a gavel, and Sequoia slid the envelope under the flour tin. Outside, the mesa held the last orange light, and the onions hissed in the pan.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
A) Curious, as a girl delights in uncovering a family secret
B) Intrigued, with only a faint undercurrent of unease
C) Nostalgic, as the galley's long history at sea is recalled
D) Uneasy, with a brief flicker of guilty curiosity

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
봉투를 세 번이나 접어 작게 만들고, 첫 줄만 읽었는데 맥박이 귀에서 울리며, 국자 소리에 놀라 봉투를 밀가루 통 밑에 숨기는 장면이 불안을 주된 정서로 만든다. 고모에게 누가 편지를 쓰는지 잠깐 궁금해하는 문장은 부차적인 호기심이다. 따라서 불안이 중심이고 죄책감 섞인 호기심이 잠깐 비치는 D가 정답이다. A는 덜 두드러진 호기심만 말하고, B는 두 정서의 비중을 뒤집었으며, C는 배의 내력이라는 소재에 기댔지만 그리움의 단서가 약하다.
### lit40-medium-02-002 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood
[지문]
Some objects refuse to leave with their owners. When I bought the house above the tide pools in Maui, Mika, the gardener, came with it, and so did a cracked snorkel mask hanging on a nail by the salt-water pool. I offered to throw it out. Mika looked at the mask the way one looks at a sleeping dog, then said that Moira, who had lived here thirty years, used it every dawn, even after she could no longer swim far. I laughed, a little embarrassed, and admitted I had already tried it on. Mika laughed too, which surprised us both. Now I glance at that nail whenever the tide fills the pool, and I find myself rinsing the mask, though I never wear it. Mika trims the hibiscus along the wall on Thursdays.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
A) Wistful, softened by brief moments of shared humor
B) Amused, with only a passing touch of sadness
C) Playful, centered on an awkward joke between strangers
D) Practical, focused on what to keep or throw away

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
가드너가 마스크를 잠든 개를 보듯 바라보고 떠난 Moira의 새벽 습관을 전하는 장면, 그리고 화자가 쓰지도 않는 마스크를 계속 헹구는 장면이 그리움을 중심 정서로 만든다. 두 사람이 함께 웃는 장면은 그 정서를 잠시 부드럽게 하는 유머다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 비중을 뒤집었고, C는 덜 두드러진 유머만 말하며, D는 버릴지 말지라는 소재에만 기대 단서가 약하다.
### lit40-medium-02-003 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood
[지문]
Tbilisi in February smelled of wet stone and glue, at least inside the bookbinder's workshop where our chess club met after closing. Dainius walked in that evening as though eleven years were a short errand. He set his coat on the press and asked whether the board by the window was free. Nobody answered. I was Tatiana, his oldest rival, so the question was really mine, and I found my hands squaring a stack of signatures that were already square. He offered no reason for leaving, and I did not ask; asking would have meant admitting I had counted the years. Still, I pushed the white pieces toward him, the way I always had when he was losing. Behind us the binder pulled thread through a spine, slow and even.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
A) Warm, as old rivals happily resume a familiar game
B) Guarded, with an undercurrent of reluctant affection
C) Affectionate, with only a slight trace of wariness
D) Mournful, as the narrator grieves the lost years of play

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
아무도 대답하지 않는 침묵, 이미 가지런한 종이를 괜히 정리하는 손, 세월을 세어 왔다는 것을 인정하기 싫어 묻지 않는 태도가 경계심을 주된 정서로 만든다. 그러면서도 예전처럼 백 기물을 상대에게 밀어 주는 행동에 마지못한 애정이 깔려 있다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 덜 두드러진 따뜻함만 말하고, C는 비중을 뒤집었으며, D는 지나간 세월이라는 소재에 기댔지만 슬픔의 단서가 약하다.
### lit40-medium-02-004 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood
[지문]
By four this morning I was already at the bakery, Esperanza, kneading before the ovens were warm, because I could not stay in the house another hour. You asked how the division went. On paper, perfectly: my brother takes the upper floor and the boathouse, I keep the kitchen and our mother's piano, and the lawyer called it a model settlement. I suppose I should be glad that no one shouted. Yet when I carried my half of the plates down the stairs, each stack seemed to weigh more than the last, and I caught myself setting out two cups out of habit. Snow is falling on the harbor now in Tromso, and the first loaves are browning. I will write again when the shop closes. Yours, Jens

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
A) Relieved, as a difficult division ends without a quarrel
B) Content, with only a slight trace of lingering sorrow
C) Heavyhearted, with only a faint sense of relief
D) Anxious, as the writer worries about the bakery's future

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
집에 한 시간도 더 머물 수 없어 새벽에 빵집으로 나온 것, 접시 더미가 점점 무겁게 느껴지고 습관처럼 컵 두 개를 놓는 장면이 무거운 상실감을 중심 정서로 만든다. 아무도 소리치지 않아 다행이라는 문장은 옅은 안도감일 뿐이다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 덜 두드러진 안도만 말하고, B는 비중을 뒤집었으며, D는 빵집이라는 소재에 기댔지만 걱정의 단서가 없다.
### lit40-medium-02-005 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters
[지문]
I unfolded the scarf on the barge's narrow deck while the Red River slid brown and slow beneath us in Hanoi. It was mustard yellow, the one color I had refused to wear since childhood, and Faris, my younger brother's tutor, watched my face as though it were an exam he had studied for. My brother must have told him yellow was my favorite; my brother thought jokes were a form of love. I tied the scarf at my throat and said it matched the lanterns on the far bank. Faris let out a breath and began explaining, too quickly, how well the boy was doing with fractions. I nodded at every fraction. Along the bank, a woman was hanging fish to dry on a line of bamboo poles.

[질문] Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between the narrator, Kainoa, and Faris?
A) Faris is relieved, while Kainoa is indifferent to his nervous efforts.
B) Kainoa seeks Faris's approval as she anxiously studies his face.
C) They are rivals competing for the younger brother's affection.
D) Faris anxiously seeks Kainoa's approval, and she kindly spares him.

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
Faris가 시험을 치르듯 Kainoa의 얼굴을 살피는 장면과, 그녀가 싫어하는 색의 스카프를 매고 칭찬하자 그가 숨을 내쉬며 급히 동생의 수학 실력을 설명하는 장면을 이어 읽으면 관계가 드러난다. Faris는 그녀의 인정을 원하고, Kainoa는 그의 마음을 상하지 않게 배려한다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A는 Kainoa의 배려를 무시하고 한쪽 감정만 반영했고, B는 지문의 face·studied를 쓰지만 방향이 반대이며, C는 지문 근거 없는 통념이다.
### lit40-medium-02-006 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters
[지문]
Agnes had not expected anyone to find her in the courtyard, where the fountain had been dry since before her family moved to Colombo. She was scraping lichen from its rim with a thumbnail when Rukhsana sat down beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Neither of them mentioned the assembly, or the speech Agnes had forgotten halfway through in front of the whole school. Instead Rukhsana opened a paper cone of roasted peanuts and tipped half of them into Agnes's palm, the way she had every afternoon since they were seven. Agnes ate one, then another, and felt her face cool. Overhead, a crow walked the length of the wall and dropped a twig into the empty basin.

[질문] Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Agnes and Rukhsana?
A) Rukhsana stays loyal to Agnes and tactfully avoids the subject of the speech.
B) Agnes feels ashamed and wishes Rukhsana would leave her alone in the courtyard.
C) Agnes comforts Rukhsana by sharing peanuts as she has since they were seven.
D) They are new acquaintances who bond over a shared dislike of the school.

Once, in a Galician spring, the river climbed
into the cellar of the old clinic, and Rafael,
the night nurse, waded down with a lantern
to carry up the jars of plum preserve
he had meant as a gift for Esteban in bed seven.
Esteban, who could not lift a spoon by then,
looked at the dripping jar a long time
and pushed it back across the blanket.
Keep it, he said. You saved it. It is yours.
Rafael set it on the sill and understood:
in that room where the water kept rising,
the old man's pride still kept its head above water.
The rain went on all night against the shutters.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “kept its head above water” most nearly suggests that Esteban's pride
A) survived despite his growing weakness and dependence.
B) made him fear that the flood would reach his room.
C) turned into anger at Rafael for entering the cellar.
D) gave him hope of recovering enough to leave the clinic.

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
Esteban은 숟가락도 들 수 없을 만큼 쇠약했지만, Rafael이 물에 잠긴 지하실에서 건져 온 선물을 고맙다고 받지 않고 네가 구했으니 네 것이라며 돌려준다. 물이 차오르는 방이라는 배경과 겹친 이 비유는 몸이 무너져 가는 상황에서도 그의 자존심이 꺾이지 않고 버티고 있음을 뜻한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 홍수를 문자 그대로 읽었고, C는 분노의 근거가 없으며, D는 회복에 대한 희망을 지문이 보여 주지 않는다.
